summary: Defines Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes used by the Open Mobile Alliance Broadcast (BCAST) service and content protection specification, which delivers broadcast content to mobile devices. It documents these attributes so they are registered and publicly described. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This paper lists special labels that phones use to describe a broadcast show, like TV on a phone, so everyone understands the same labels.

subtitle: SDP attributes for describing broadcast services on mobile devices.

tldr.problem: The Open Mobile Alliance's Broadcast (OMA BCAST) specification defines broadcast services delivered to mobile devices via 3GPP, 3GPP2, and DVB-H networks, and it needs to communicate service parameters and content protection settings to clients using the Session Description Protocol (SDP).
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers four new SDP attributes defined by the OMA BCAST specification: bcastversion (broadcast system version), stkmstream (short-term key message stream identifier), SRTPAuthentication (SRTP authentication algorithm), and SRTPROCTxRate (SRTP rollover counter transmission rate). These allow broadcast servers to signal configuration parameters to clients.
tldr.outcome: The attributes are formally registered with IANA in the SDP parameters registry, making them public and unambiguous for use by broadcast systems and compliant media players.

today: RFC 5159 is Informational and remains the definition of these SDP attributes for OMA BCAST systems. It has not been obsoleted. These attributes enable broadcast servers to signal service and content protection parameters to mobile device clients.

sections.title: OMA Broadcast and SDP
sections.content:
The Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) is a standards body for mobile and wireless services. Its Broadcast (BCAST) group specifies mechanisms for broadcasting services and protecting content over mobile networks. Broadcast services include live or on-demand multimedia content (video, audio) delivered to mobile devices through 3GPP Multimedia Broadcast/Multicast Service (MBMS), 3GPP2 Broadcast and Multicast Services (BCMCS), or Digital Video Broadcasting - Handheld (DVB-H).

To coordinate these services, the broadcast server must communicate service parameters and content protection settings to receiving clients. The Session Description Protocol (RFC 4566), which describes multimedia sessions, is used for this signaling. Per RFC 4566, new SDP attributes must be registered through IANA with name, contact information, and description. A standards-track specification is typically recommended for widely-deployed attributes, but in this case IETF chose to use a non-standards-track RFC because OMA maintains change control of the BCAST specification that defines the interpretation of attribute values.
sections.plainLanguage: OMA BCAST is a system for sending broadcast TV and radio to phones. The phone needs to understand what kind of broadcast it's getting and how to decrypt it. The broadcast server sends this info using special labels called SDP attributes.

sections.title: Terminology and SDP Attributes
sections.content:
The RFC uses RFC 2119 keywords (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) to clarify recommendations. It registers four new SDP attributes, all of which are defined in the OMA-TS-BCAST_SvcCntProtection specification.

bcastversion is a session-level attribute that specifies the OMA BCAST version in the format x.y, where x and y are non-negative decimal numbers. This tells the client which broadcast system version is in use. The attribute value is mandatory and of XML data type decimal. This allows future broadcast systems to signal which version is being used, and if a downgrade occurs, it could be exploited for downgrade attacks on older implementations, so the SDP should be protected.

stkmstream is a session-level or media-level attribute that specifies the identifier of a Short-Term Key Message stream. Each session or media stream can have multiple stkmstream attributes. The value is a unique non-zero integer identifying a particular key stream. The attribute is optional and is only present when encrypted media streams need to indicate which key stream to listen to for decryption. When it appears at the media level, it overrides any session-level stkmstream attribute for that media.

SRTPAuthentication is a media-level attribute that identifies which authentication algorithm is used when Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) is employed. It takes an integer identifier for an SRTP authentication algorithm value. Three integrity transforms are registered: value 2 for RCCm1, 3 for RCCm2, and 4 for RCCm3.

SRTPROCTxRate is a media-level attribute that defines the SRTP Rollover Counter (ROC) transmission rate, R. It takes a decimal integer value between 1 and 65535. If not included in the negotiation, the default value is 1. This controls how frequently the encryption state counter is transmitted to synchronize encryption between server and clients.
sections.plainLanguage: Four labels: bcastversion tells what system version, stkmstream says which encryption key stream to use, SRTPAuthentication says which encryption method, SRTPROCTxRate says how often to sync the encryption counter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes several security concerns in addition to those covered in RFC 4566 section 7. The bcastversion parameter could be exploited for downgrade attacks if left unprotected. An attacker could modify the version number to force the client to use an older, less secure broadcast system version. Servers should protect the SDP description to prevent such attacks.

The stkmstream parameter provides references to key management streams, allowing receivers to map media streams to the encryption streams and retrieve the keys needed to decrypt content. If unprotected, this parameter could be modified to cause denial-of-service attacks by directing clients to listen to wrong key streams or non-existent streams, resulting in decryption failures or system confusion.

These security considerations emphasize that the SDP description itself should be authenticated and encrypted, or at least integrity-protected, when used in a broadcast service where content protection is required.
sections.plainLanguage: If an attacker changes the version number, the phone might use worse encryption. If the attacker changes the key stream ID, the phone can't decrypt the broadcast. So the broadcast description should be signed or encrypted to prevent tampering.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content:
The RFC formally registers all four attributes in the Session Description Protocol Parameters registry maintained by IANA, following the template format specified in RFC 4566. Each attribute registration includes:

  • Contact information for the registrant (in this case, Anja Jerichow at Nokia Siemens Networks)
  • The attribute name (e.g., bcastversion)
  • A long-form description (e.g., 'BCAST version')
  • The type of attribute (session-level or media-level)
  • Whether it depends on character set
  • The purpose and meaning of the attribute
  • The specification of attribute values (syntax and semantics)

The registration also notes that these attributes are defined in the OMA specification document OMA-TS-BCAST_SvcCntProtection and that further details can be found there. By registering these attributes, any future RFC or standard that needs to refer to OMA broadcast parameters can use these well-known names and meanings rather than inventing their own, promoting interoperability across the broadcast ecosystem.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps a registry of all SDP attributes. This document adds four new ones to the list with official names, descriptions, and what they mean, so everyone uses the same labels.
